summary: This RFC describes extending a network's broadcast domain over more than one physical network by using a broadcast packet repeater.

eli5.summary: A relay that repeats a shout from one room into the next room so more people can hear.

questions: how to extend broadcast over multiple networks
what is a broadcast packet repeater
subtitle: A broadcast repeater mechanism that extends broadcast messages across multiple physical networks.

tldr.problem: Local area network broadcasts only reach hosts on the same physical network. Applications like the Cronus distributed operating system need to broadcast across multiple LANs connected by gateways, but broadcast packets do not cross gateway boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: A broadcast repeater is a user-level process on a network host that listens for broadcast packets, selectively forwards them over a TCP connection to repeaters on distant LANs, and rebroadcasts them locally while preserving the original source address. The repeater can filter packets by port number or other header fields.
tldr.outcome: The authors implemented and tested the broadcast repeater on VAX running 4.2 BSD Unix, extending the broadcast domain across two Ethernets separated by two other LANs. The mechanism proved useful but imposes overhead on the host running it.

today: RFC 947 is informational. The broadcast repeater concept was a pragmatic solution to a specific limitation in 1985. Modern networking largely addresses these concerns through multicast protocols (like IGMP) and more sophisticated application-level techniques, reducing the need for broadcast-based inter-network communication.

sections.title: The Broadcast Problem Across Networks
sections.content:
When multiple LANs are connected by Internet gateways, broadcast packets sent on one LAN do not reach hosts on the other LANs. This is by design: gateways forward individual unicast packets addressed to specific hosts but do not forward broadcast packets, which are addressed to everyone on a single physical network.

For the Cronus distributed operating system, this was a limitation. Cronus uses broadcasting to dynamically locate resources and collect status information from servers. The designers needed to extend broadcasting across multiple LANs without modifying gateways or the Cronus kernel itself. A multicast mechanism would have been more appropriate, but it was unavailable on some of their network implementations.
sections.eli5: A message shouted on one network does not reach another network, even if a gateway connects them. Cronus needs shouts to reach everywhere, so the team invented a relay.

sections.title: The Broadcast Repeater Solution
sections.content:
A broadcast repeater is a process on a network host that listens for broadcast packets matching certain criteria—for example, UDP packets destined to specific ports used by Cronus. When such a packet arrives, the forwarder process encapsulates it and sends it via TCP to repeater processes on foreign networks. Each remote repeater rebroadcasts the packet on its local LAN using that LAN's link-level broadcast address, preserving the original packet's source address.

The repeater reads a configuration file on startup specifying which repeater processes to contact and which packets to forward to each one. The forwarder also handles feedback prevention: it does not connect to repeaters on the same LAN, and it does not forward packets whose source is not on its own LAN. This prevents broadcast loops.
sections.eli5: The repeater listens to broadcasts, picks the ones it should forward (like Cronus messages), wraps them up, sends them over TCP to another repeater far away, and that repeater unwraps and reshouts them locally.

sections.title: Implementation and Performance
sections.content:
The broadcast repeater was implemented as two separate processes: a forwarder that listens for and captures packets, and a repeater that receives and rebroadcasts them. The implementation required a special capability in the BBN TCP/IP stack to send IP packets with another host's source address.

Testing on VAX running 4.2 BSD Unix proved successful: the repeater extended the broadcast domain to include two Ethernets physically separated by two other LANs. However, the repeater imposes significant overhead on the host running it because the forwarder is woken for every UDP packet arriving at the host, with filtering decisions made in user-level software. The authors suggest moving the implementation to a dedicated microcomputer as a better-suited platform.
sections.eli5: It worked! Two separate computer groups could shout to each other across four networks. But waking up for every message was tiring for the computer, so moving it to a special box would be better.

references.text: Mogul, J., "Toward an Internet Standard Scheme for Subnetting," RFC 940.
